pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) THE SMOKING GUN: The triad of severe neuro-visceral pain disproportionate to exam findings, SIADH-induced hyponatremia, and fresh amber urine oxidizing to a dark port-wine color under light, triggered by fasting and a sulfonamide antibiotic. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute Intermittent Porphyria is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD) in the heme biosynthesis pathway. When hepatic heme requirements spike—precipitated here by CYP450 induction from trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ALAS1 disinhibition from caloric fasting—the rate-limiting enzyme ALAS1 is violently upregulated. The metabolic bottleneck results in massive neurotoxic accumulation of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). These neurotoxins damage the autonomic system (severe abdominal colic, hypertension, tachycardia), peripheral motor nerves (descending or ascending motor paralysis), and the central nervous system (delirium, hypothalamic SIADH causing severe hyponatremia). When exposed to light and air, excessive colorless PBG in the urine polymerizes into porphobilin and porphyrins, revealing the pathognomonic dark port-wine discoloration. Treatment requires immediate cessation of inducing drugs, intravenous dextrose to suppress ALAS1, and urgent IV hemin administration.
